paras: The lynching of James Waters was the killing of a Black farmhand by a mob of about 150 men in Johnson County, Georgia, in mid-May 1919, after he was accused of attacking a white girl. The men took Waters from a deputy sheriff who was driving him to the Macon jail, tied him to a tree and shot him, and a coroner's inquest attributed his death to unknown persons. The Chicago Defender reported a different account in which Waters denied the charge, which it linked to his plan to leave his employer's farm.

Waters had worked on a farm owned by the parents of the girl who accused him and, according to a Dublin dispatch, was regarded as trustworthy. He was accused of attacking her about two weeks before his death, disappeared soon afterward, and was captured at Sun Hill in Washington County; officers said he confessed.

The Defender's Dublin correspondent gave another account of the charge. By that report, Waters had told the farmer who had employed him for several years that he was leaving, which angered the farmer, and the sheriff then arrested Waters on a charge of attempted assault on the farmer's daughter. Waters denied the charge and pointed to his years of service on the farm.

According to Deputy Sheriff O. L. Smith, he was taking Waters by automobile to the jail at Macon for safekeeping when he found an automobile across the road at a bridge over the Ohoopee River in Johnson County. As he stopped, about 150 men came out of the roadside bushes and pointed guns at him, took the prisoner from the car, and ordered the deputy to drive on. Waters's body was later found tied to a tree with ropes and riddled with bullets; the mob had not hanged him, and some of the ropes had been cut by the shots.
The Defender's version placed the handover at the county jail, where it said a mob had gathered and the sheriff turned Waters over to it without any attempt to protect him.

A coroner's inquest, held the same day according to the Planet's dispatch and the next day according to the Defender, found that Waters died at the hands of unknown persons. The Defender added that, 'on good authority', the coroner's jury had been drawn from the men who made up the mob, and that hundreds of Black residents were preparing to leave. No report of arrests or prosecution appears in the coverage.

The Black press carried two versions of the killing. The wire dispatch, based on the deputy's account, ran in the St. Louis Argus on May 23 under the headline 'Girl's Assailant Lynched', with the victim's name given as 'James Walters', and in the Richmond Planet on May 24 as 'Colored Man Is Shot to Death by Angry Georgian Mob'. Both kept the dispatch's wording about the officers' claim of a confession, and the Planet's text referred to the accuser as 'his victim'.

The Chicago Defender of May 24 headlined its own Dublin item 'Wanted to Leave Farm: Is Lynched', gave Waters's denial, faulted the sheriff, and called the killing 'this horrible murder'. The same day the Cleveland Advocate reprinted a metropolitan daily's editorial that cited the Constitution's Dublin correspondent for the detail that the prisoner was 'literally shot to pieces'. That editorial denounced the mob as an attack on 'the law' and 'intolerable business' while stating that it had 'no reason to doubt the guilt of the victim'.

Earlier, on May 17, a Savannah Tribune editorial calling Black readers to an NAACP meeting spoke of Wrightsville, Georgia, 'where the last Negro victim of the hating Georgia mob was slaughtered without show of trial', without naming the victim.

The Planet's May 15 dispatch said Waters was killed 'today', while the Argus's May 21 dispatch said 'last Wednesday', which would be May 14. The confession rests on the officers' word and the bridge ambush on the deputy's own account, while the Defender's version of a denial and a handover by the sheriff came from an unnamed source in a badly printed item.

Waters was taken from an officer by about 150 armed men and shot to death while tied to a tree (A3, A6), on an accusation of attacking a white girl (A3, A6, A4), with no legal authority.

accounts.label: Wire report (deputy's account)
accounts.gist: Waters, captured at Sun Hill and said by officers to have confessed, was being driven to the Macon jail when about 150 armed men stopped Deputy O. L. Smith at an Ohoopee River bridge, took Waters, tied him to a tree and shot him; an inquest found death at the hands of unknown persons.

accounts.label: Constitution's Dublin correspondent, via a reprinted editorial
accounts.gist: A mob with 150 rifles took the prisoner from a deputy at a river bridge, bound him to a tree and 'literally shot to pieces' his body, which passersby found.

accounts.label: Chicago Defender's Dublin item
accounts.gist: Waters had told the farmer who had employed him for years that he was leaving, angering him; he was then charged with attempted assault on the farmer's daughter, denied it, and was turned over to a waiting mob without protection by the sheriff; the coroner's jury was said to be drawn from the mob.

framing.detail: The St. Louis Argus ran the dispatch under 'Girl's Assailant Lynched', treating the accusation as fact in the headline, alongside items on other lynchings.
The Richmond Planet headlined 'Colored Man Is Shot to Death by Angry Georgian Mob' but kept the wire's 'his victim' and the officers' claim of a confession.
The Chicago Defender headlined 'Wanted to Leave Farm: Is Lynched', gave Waters's denial, accused the sheriff of offering no protection, and called it 'this horrible murder'.

The Cleveland Advocate reprinted a metropolitan daily's editorial that called the killing 'an assault upon the law' and 'intolerable business' while saying it had 'no reason to doubt the guilt of the victim'.
The Savannah Tribune's editorial spoke of a victim 'slaughtered without show of trial' at Wrightsville, Georgia, in calling for an NAACP meeting.
